planting.note: Plant a container or balled tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; as an all-male clone, Kingan is propagated only from cuttings and never sets fruit.

directions: Kingan is an all-male white mulberry selection grown strictly for fast, dense shade rather than fruit, since male clones produce only inconspicuous catkins and set no berries. It grows quickly into a broad, vase-shaped canopy and tolerates heat, drought, poor alkaline soil, and road salt better than most shade trees, making it a reliable choice for difficult urban sites. Because surface roots can be aggressive, keep it away from paving, septic lines, and foundations. Light structural pruning while young helps develop strong scaffold branches on what becomes a large, fast-growing tree.

planting.note: Plant a container or balled tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; propagate only from cuttings, since Bellaire is an all-male clone that will never produce fruit.

directions: Bellaire is a fruitless white mulberry clone distinguished by a tendency toward multiple trunks arising low on the plant, giving mature specimens a denser, more clumping silhouette than single-trunk fruitless types. Grown for its fast-forming, heat- and drought-tolerant shade canopy, it never produces berries, so it is favored near patios and parking areas where fruit drop would otherwise stain pavement. It adapts to a wide range of soils, including poor or alkaline ground, once established. Thin or select a dominant trunk while the tree is young if a more traditional single-stem shade tree form is preferred.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (ENH-567, Morus alba Fruitless Cultivars)

planting.note: Plant a container or balled tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hempton is an all-male clone propagated by cuttings and sets no fruit.

directions: Hempton is another named fruitless white mulberry clone bred for dense, dark-green summer canopy without the staining berry drop of seedling trees, forming a rounded mass of foliage from a short trunk. Like other fruitless mulberry selections it is fast-growing and tough, shrugging off heat, drought, and poor soil, but its surface roots can heave nearby pavement and it is more prone to ice and storm damage than slower-growing shade trees. It drops leaves somewhat earlier in late summer than many shade trees, so plan for a shorter autumn canopy display. Best used where quick, low-maintenance shade matters more than fall color or longevity.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (ENH-567, Morus alba Fruitless Cultivars)

planting.note: Plant a container or balled tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Urban is an all-male clone propagated only by cuttings and never bears fruit.

directions: Urban is a fruitless white mulberry clone selected specifically for exceptional tolerance of air pollution, compacted soil, and reflected heat, which made it a favorite street and parking-lot tree in mid-twentieth-century municipal plantings. It grows into a wide, spreading canopy with mostly unlobed, glossy leaves that turn yellow in fall, and like other male clones produces no messy fruit drop. Growth is notably fast, often ten feet or more a year while young, so early structural pruning is important to prevent weak, storm-prone branch unions. Give it plenty of root and canopy room, since its spread can exceed its height at maturity.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension (ENH-567, Morus alba Fruitless Cultivars)
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant a container tree in spring in well-drained clay, loam, or sandy soil in full sun; Townsend tolerates drought once established and needs no second tree to fruit.

directions: Townsend is a selection of the native American red mulberry prized for its erect, oval growth habit, which is tidier than the sprawling form typical of wild red mulberry seedlings. It bears abundant slender, elongated black fruit resembling a slim blackberry, with a sweet flavor, and is noticeably more cold-hardy than true black mulberry, surviving winters well into the upper Midwest and mid-Atlantic. Established trees handle clay and sandy soils and tolerate drought, needing little care beyond an annual shaping prune to control size. Site it well away from driveways, patios, and parked cars, since dropped fruit stains readily and the tree is best treated as a naturalized or wildlife planting rather than a formal specimen.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox (Morus rubra 'Townsend')

planting.note: Plant an own-root container tree in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jerusalem is self-fertile and needs no second tree.

directions: Jerusalem was propagated in the early 2000s by Israeli nurseryman Omer Hochberg from a tree growing near the city of Jerusalem and brought into UK cultivation shortly after; it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable crops of richly flavored, deep black fruit typical of true black mulberry. Like other Morus nigra selections it grows slowly into a low, broad, long-lived tree, usually on its own roots rather than grafted, and takes a few years to settle into full production. Established trees tolerate heat and are easy-care once rooted in, needing only occasional deep watering during dry spells and light pruning to maintain shape. Because ripe fruit drops and stains heavily, site it away from paths, patios, and parked vehicles.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society (Award of Garden Merit records)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree after the last frost in full sun in well-drained soil; self-fertile, so a single tree crops on its own.

directions: Australian Green is a trade name for a long-fruited, shahtoot-type mulberry grown for berries that ripen to a greenish-yellow rather than the usual black or red, with a distinctive sweet flavor many growers compare to honeydew melon rather than typical mulberry tartness. Fruit is long and slender like other shahtoot-type mulberries, and because it never darkens fully, ripe berries are harder to judge by color alone — picking when fruit softens and detaches easily from the stem gives the best flavor. The tree fruits readily in warm climates and benefits from regular moisture during fruit swell to maximize size and sweetness. As with other mulberries, expect heavy bird interest and site the tree away from paving since the fruit, while pale, still drops and can stain.
